chapters.title: The Moth and the Flame
paragraphs: Byomkesh Babu, do you think the police ever hear of every case of poisoning in our country? You don’t even need a doctor’s certificate to cremate a corpse. Perhaps if someone of importance is poisoned, there’s a bit of an uproar. Even then, the family hushes it up. Yet I believe the number of poisonings in this country is not at all insignificant.”
Byomkesh, drawing deeply on his hookah, said after a pause, “Tell me, all these poisons and narcotics you people seize—where do they end up?”

Pandeyji replied, “Where else would they go? They stay with us for a while, then are sent to the head office, and they take care of it. But that’s just a fraction. Most of it is out there, circulating in the black market. Whoever needs it, buys it and uses it.” Pandeyji sighed—“War and revolution strip civilized men of their civility. Then the mask of conscience and reason falls away, and the raw, ravenous beast emerges. How fragile our civilization is! At heart, we are barbarians.”

Byomkesh seemed to weigh the words, then said, “Indeed, we are barbarians. But when we regress from civilization to barbarism, we take with us at least one trait of civilization. The mask doesn’t fall so easily, Pandeyji; it takes time to uncover the beast within. Outwardly, a calm, gentle, harmless creature—inside, sharp claws and fangs. That is the most terrifying thing of all.”
The clock struck eight. It was a winter night, but we felt no particular urge to return home; so when Pandeyji proposed another round of tea, we did not object.
At that moment, the servant entered and announced, “Inspector Chowdhury has arrived.”
Pandeyji said, “Who—Ratikanta? Bring him in. And prepare four cups of tea.”

The servant departed. A moment later, a young man in police uniform entered. Tall and sturdy, with a ruddy complexion, sharp features, and blue eyes—at first glance, one might mistake him for a sahib. He was about thirty. He came in, raised his right hand in a salute, and stood beside Pandeyji.
Pandeyji asked, “What news, Ratikanta?”

Ratikanta replied, “Sir, there’s an invitation letter.” Saying this, he produced an envelope from his overcoat pocket. Ratikanta’s speech was pure Hindi of northern India, not the adulterated dialect of Bihar.
Pandeyji smiled and said, “What’s the invitation for? Your wedding, perhaps?”
Ratikanta made a woeful face and replied, “Who would marry me, sir? It’s an invitation from Dipanarayan Singh.”
As Pandeyji opened the envelope, he said, “But why did you bring Dipanarayan Singh’s invitation?”

Ratikanta, with a playful, embarrassed smile, said, “What can I do, sir? He’s a big man, a relative—might become a minister someday, so I have to keep up appearances. I drop by now and then to pay my respects. Went today, and he handed me all the invitation letters for the police officers to deliver.”
Pandeyji drew out a glossy card embossed in gold and read it. “Hmm, looks like a serious affair. A proper dinner. But what’s the occasion?”
Ratikanta replied, “He’s recovered after a long illness, so he’s treating his friends. He’s invited all the city’s notables.”
Pandeyji, slipping the card back into the envelope, said, “The invitation is for tomorrow night. But—”
Bahni-Patanga 513
“I won’t be able to come, Ratikanta.”
“Why, sir? Are you going out for inspection tomorrow?”
“No. These two gentlemen have come from Calcutta, I’ve invited them for dinner tomorrow night.”
Byomkesh murmured softly, “Kashmiri chicken korma.”

Ratikanta glanced at us with a sudden smile. All this while, he had been casting curious glances our way; perhaps he was intrigued to see us, unfamiliar faces, sitting with Panditji and drawing on the hookah, but he had not let his curiosity show. Now, smiling, he raised his right hand to his forehead in a salute. Then he said to Panditji, “Huzoor, if I’d known about the Kashmiri korma, I’d have come to your house tomorrow to join the adda myself. But now there’s no way. Well, I’ll take your leave for today.”
Panditji said, “Sit, have some tea before you go.”

Ratikanta replied, “Tea can wait for another day, huzoor. And if you serve Kashmiri korma, there’s nothing more to say. But I really can’t stay today. I still have two or three letters left to deliver. Besides, I have to go report to Dipnarayanji. You saw the RSVP written on the invitation, didn’t you?”
“All right, then, go on.”
With a gentle smile, Ratikanta saluted all of us together and took his leave.
Byomkesh exclaimed, “Ah, what a striking young man! Like a prince!”

Panditji said, “You’re not far from the truth. His ancestors were great taluqdars of Pratapgarh. Almost royalty. Now their fortunes have fallen so low that Ratikanta had to take up a job. He’s a clever boy; educated himself through his own efforts, passed his B.Sc.”
Byomkesh said, “These days, it’s a good sign that sons of noble houses are joining the police.”
The tea arrived. After some conversation on other topics, Byomkesh asked, “Who is Dipnarayan Singh?”

Panditji replied, “You haven’t heard of Dipnarayan Singh? A formidable zamindar of Bihar, annual income of a million rupees, and on top of that, he deals in moneylending. But he’s a good man. He supported the political movement with funds. Now he’s getting on in years, close to fifty—” He took a few puffs on the hookah and continued, “In his old age, he’s made one mistake: he’s taken a young bride.”
“Is the former wife still living?”

“No, not that. The former wife passed away a few years ago, and after that, the young bride arrived. One can’t really blame the gentleman—no children, only a nephew who shares the estate, but he’s utterly useless. Someone must enjoy all this royal splendor, after all.”
“Then what’s the mistake in Dipnarayan Singh marrying again? The family line will be preserved.”
“The line isn’t preserved yet. But that’s not the main point. The real issue is that Dipnarayan Singh, smitten by beauty, married outside his caste. A civil marriage.”
“The young bride is beautiful, I suppose?”
“Beautiful and accomplished. Skilled in the arts, she can sing and dance, she can paint, and on top of that, she’s a brilliant student from Allahabad University—first class first in her B.A.”
“Dipnarayan Singh seems both fortunate and progressive.”
Byomkesh Samagra
“He wasn’t always this progressive. Until recently, the women in his household lived behind the purdah. Now, the veil has been lifted entirely.”
“Well, that’s good, isn’t it? What’s wrong with that?”

“There’s nothing wrong. But the unfamiliarity stings, like a drop of acid on the forehead. The people of Bihar still haven’t been able to cast off the purdah from their hearts. So, the moment they see women with a bit of freedom, they start whispering, exchanging knowing glances—”

Our conversation, following the path of women’s emancipation, soon veered into the realm of politics; the hands of the clock were inching steadily towards nine. If I returned home too late at night, Satyabati would raise a ruckus. So, with some reluctance, we prepared to take our leave.
Pandeyji said, “Come, let me drop you off in my car.” He used to have a motorcycle; now he had acquired a small motorcar.

We had just risen to our feet when, from the corner of the room, the telephone began to ring. Pandeyji went to answer—“Hello… Yes, this is Purandar Pandey… You wish to speak to Dipnarayan Singh?… Namaste, namaste… I very much wanted to attend your party, but… Bring my friends along as well?… Well—they’re still here, let me ask them—”
Covering the mouthpiece with his hand, Pandeyji turned to us. “Dipnarayan Singh is inviting you both to his party as well. What do you say?”
Byomkesh glanced at me, then said, “Why not! It’ll be something new. Your Kashmiri korma will have to wait for now.”
Smiling, Pandeyji spoke into the telephone, “Very well, they’ll come… Please send their cards to me… Yes, we’ll meet again tomorrow. Namaste.”
Replacing the receiver, Pandeyji said, “Come, let me drop you home now.”
TWO
The following evening, around seven, Pandeyji arrived and bundled us into his car, taking us to Dipnarayan Singh’s house.

Dipnarayan Singh’s residence was in the old quarter of the city—a sprawling, two-storied house from a bygone era, surrounded by high walls like a prison. When we arrived, we saw the house and garden aglow with Japanese lanterns, the faint strains of a shehnai drifting through the air, and a crowd of guests already assembled.

The main gathering was in the large hall on the ground floor, though guests were seated in the surrounding rooms as well. In one room, a bridge adda was underway; in another, elderly, official-looking guests had formed their own exclusive circle and were deep in conversation. Liveried servants, their uniforms adorned with badges, circulated with trays of tea, coffee, and stronger drinks.

The hall itself was vast, furnished in the English style with sofa sets arranged here and there. Each sofa set hosted its own little group. In the center of the room, facing the main door, was a divan-like seat. Reclining against its cushions sat a middle-aged man—this was our host, Dipnarayan Singh. He wore a long, warm coat and a woolen scarf around his neck. His features were pleasant; at fifty, he had not yet succumbed to the stiffness of age, though the pallor and gauntness of his face suggested he was only recently recovering from a long illness. With utmost courtesy, he rose and shook our hands in both of his.
Bohni - Patanga 515
Pandeyji said, “Congratulations on your recovery.”

Dipnarayan smiled sweetly, his face still gaunt. “Many thanks. I had no hope of surviving, Pandeyji. If it weren’t for Dr. Palit, I wouldn’t have made it this time.” He gestured toward a corner of the room.

In the corner, seated alone on a sofa, was a gentleman in coat and trousers—of medium build, his attire lacking any particular elegance, about fifty years old by estimate. Noticing the gesture, he came over and stood before us. Introductions were made. Dipnarayan Singh said, “It is thanks to him that I have been granted a new lease on life.”

Dr. Palit seemed a little embarrassed. He was a man of grave disposition. After a brief silence, he said, “I did nothing more than what is required of a doctor. Besides, though I treated him, all the eminent doctors of the city examined him as well. Mr. Tridib—”
Pandeyji asked, “What was the illness?”

From the symptoms Dr. Palit described, in the manner of Western medical science, I gathered that a variety of malignant germs had conspired with the liver to cause anemia and were on the verge of injuring the heart. It had taken injections and other infernal treatments to bring them under control. Now, of course, the patient’s condition was much improved, though he still required careful monitoring.

At that moment, a sound like someone blowing his nose startled us from behind. Turning, I saw a young man standing there, making a noise through his nose as if to express disdain. His face was sharp as a jackal’s, his body clad in the latest Western fashion, his expression mocking and arrogant. Dipnarayan introduced him—“This is Dr. Jagannath Prasad, a young Bihari doctor.” Dr. Jagannath nodded at us with contempt, and from the few words he spoke, it was clear that he held nothing but scorn for senior doctors, especially if they happened to be Bengali. Had the responsibility for Dipnarayan Singh’s treatment been entrusted to him instead of to a handful of elderly Bengali doctors, he would have cured the illness in five days. Dipnarayan Singh listened to him with a wry, gentle smile. Dr. Palit, annoyed, returned to his seat. Dr. Jagannath, after a few more moments of oration, spotted a servant carrying drinks and, neighing like a horse, hurried off in that direction.

Dipnarayan Singh, in a voice tinged with both shame and resentment, said, “These are the Biharis of the new age. They have no respect for merit; under the guise of communalism, they only look out for themselves. Today, Bengalis are losing their standing in Bihar, and it is they who are to blame.”
Byomkesh said, “Perhaps the Bengalis are at fault too.”
Dipnarayan replied, “Perhaps. But the irony is, when they fall ill, when their lives hang in the balance, it is to the Bengali doctors that they run.”
This unpleasant provincial topic having arisen, we all felt a little awkward, but Pandeyji smoothed things over, changed the subject with a few words, and led us over to where Dr. Palit was seated.
Once we were settled, Dr. Palit smiled faintly and said, “What else did Horse Jagannath have to say?”
Pandeyji burst out laughing. “So his name is Horse Jagannath? Splendid name, suits him perfectly. But don’t pay any heed to their words, Doctor. Who takes them seriously anyway?”
Palit said, “But how can one not? They go about in groups, spreading their propaganda everywhere.”
BYOMKESH SAMAGRA
The clever ones may not pay them any heed, but ordinary folk listen to their every word.’

Our conversation might have continued a while longer, but suddenly it was interrupted by a strange kind of laughter from nearby. Turning my head, I saw that, not far from us, three men had settled themselves onto another sofa set. Among them, the one who was laughing so uproariously was so immense in size that he alone seemed to occupy the entire sofa. A barrel-chested, elephant-shouldered youth, with rolls of fat cascading from chin to hip in undulating waves. The bizarre laughter that issued from his throat was so peculiar, it was hard to believe that such a cacophony could emerge from a single human being—unless one witnessed it firsthand. Imagine a dozen jackals howling in unison, and, mingled with that, the wailing of several newborns snatched from their mothers—perhaps then you might begin to grasp the tumult of sound he produced.

The other two men sat silently, smirking. Curiously, the fat youth was as corpulent as his two companions were thin. If the flesh and fat of these three were distributed evenly, you might have ended up with three healthy, ordinary men. Needless to say, the thunderous laughter had drawn the startled gaze of everyone in the room.
A frail, elderly man, wearing a silk turban, appeared from somewhere and hurried towards them.
Byomkesh leaned over and whispered to Dr. Palit, ‘Who is that behemoth?’

Dr. Palit suppressed a smile and replied, ‘That’s Debnarayan, nephew of Dipnarayan Babu. An absolute—’ He left the sentence unfinished, but the unspoken noun was all too clear. It was about him that Pandeyji had remarked yesterday—“Not only is he a hopeless fool, but his wits are as bloated as his body.” The turbaned old man approached the two thin youths and whispered something in their ears, seemingly a gentle rebuke. The two thin men looked thoroughly chastened, lowering their eyes like scolded, drenched cats. The behemoth’s laughter had not yet ceased, though it was now subsiding. The old man stood behind him, bent close to his ear, and murmured something. Suddenly, like a car slamming on its brakes, the laughter came to an abrupt, jarring halt.
Byomkesh, as before, quietly asked Dr. Palit, ‘Who are the two thin fellows?’

Palit replied, ‘The one with the curly hair and crab-like moustache is Debnarayan’s buffoon—his “yar,” you could say. Name’s Beniprasad. The other is Liladhar Banshi—assistant manager of Dipnarayan Babu’s estate, and assistant buffoon to Debnarayan.’
‘And the old man?’
‘That’s Gangadhar Banshi, Liladhar’s father, the chief manager of the estate. A deep-water fish, that one.’

The deep-water fish glanced at us once, his eyes lifting, and with a gentle, honeyed smile, he anointed us before departing elsewhere. Debnarayan, meanwhile, drew from the pocket of his gleaming sharkskin bandhgala coat a massive betel nut box, stuffed several betel leaves into his mouth, and began to chew with a grave, ponderous expression. It was hard to believe this was the same man who, only moments ago, had been raising such a ruckus with his laughter.
Byomkesh asked, ‘Did you catch what was so funny?’
Palit replied, ‘I suppose the buffoons must have said something amusing, hence all that laughter.’
A servant appeared, bearing a silver tray laden with betel leaves wrapped in golden foil and cigarettes. We lit our cigarettes. Byomkesh glanced about and said to Pandeyji, ‘Inspector—’
I do not see Ratikanta.’
Pandeyji said, ‘Perhaps he is in another room. Or maybe he’s been detained at the thana. He will surely come. Please, you all sit. I’ll just have a word with the Commissioner Sahib and return.’

Pandeyji got up and left. The three of us sat there, drawing on our cigarettes, our eyes wandering over the scattered guests in the room. The majority were men, though there were one or two women among them.

At that moment, a lady entered through a door at the far end of the room. The room was already well-lit, yet it seemed that with her arrival, the brightness increased. I could not tell what color sari she wore, nor what ornaments adorned her; all I saw was a moving source of radiance slowly advancing towards us. Everyone in the room became alert at once; some even rose to their feet and greeted her with folded hands. The lady, smiling and graceful, greeted everyone as she made her way toward us.
Dr. Palit stubbed out his cigarette in the ashtray and murmured, ‘Mrs. Dipnarayan—Shakuntala.’

A true beauty. She could not be less than twenty-four or twenty-five, yet the intoxicating bloom of youth seemed to burst forth from her every limb. In the northwestern regions of our country, one might see two or four such golden-skinned, radiant women, but here they are rare. Even her name—Shakuntala—seemed to harmonize with her beauty. Shakuntala—the celestial nymph, the very one who made Dushyanta forget himself. It was not hard to understand why Dipnarayan Singh, a man of mature years, had chosen to marry outside his caste.

Shakuntala came and stood before us, and we rose respectfully. Dr. Palit introduced us. Shakuntala spoke a few words of cordial welcome in a sweet voice, her manner blending the courtesy of a mistress of the house with the modesty of a young woman. Then she turned away.

At that moment, I noticed that Shakuntala was not alone; behind her stood another young woman. Just as the morning star is lost in the sun’s brilliance, so had this young woman been hidden until now. Now I saw that she carried a child of about a year and a half in her arms. In fact, it was the child’s sudden wail that drew our attention to her. The young woman was perhaps a year or two younger than Shakuntala; fair and comely, with a plump, loose figure, she seemed almost weighed down by her costly clothes and heavy jewelry. There was abundance in her attire, but no finesse. Moreover, it seemed she was not accustomed to mingling openly with men; the veil of seclusion had not yet lifted from her.
As the child began to cry, Shakuntala turned and glanced back. A shadow of displeasure crossed her face. She said, ‘Chandni, why have you brought the boy here? Go, leave him with the nurse.’
Like a loyal dog chastised by its master, the young woman looked at Shakuntala, then, bowing her head meekly, retraced her steps with the child in her arms.
From a distance, Dipnarayan called to his wife—‘Shakuntala!’—some distinguished guests had arrived.
Shakuntala went that way. Glancing sideways, I saw Debnarayan, in his arms...
Byomkesh Samagra

With bulging, frog-like eyes, he stared at Shakuntala. We lit another cigarette. Byomkesh asked, “Who was the second lady?” Dr. Palit replied absentmindedly, “Debnarayan’s wife. The boy is Debnarayan’s as well.” I noticed a faint furrow on Dr. Palit’s brow. His gaze, too, was following Shakuntala.
We sat for a long while, passing the time in a haze of smoke. Dr. Palit remained distracted, his eyes trailing Shakuntala with a hint of unease.

At half past eight, the call for dinner arrived. In another hall, a table had been laid for the meal. The arrangements were regal. Cooks and servers had come from some British hotel in Calcutta. By the time we finished eating and rose from the table, it was a quarter to ten.

Returning to the outer hall, we busied ourselves with paan and cigarettes. Dr. Palit let out a satisfied sigh and said, “Not bad at all. Well, I’ll take my leave now—might have to go out to see a patient tonight. I’ll be back tomorrow morning to give Dipnarayan Babu his injection.”
Byomkesh asked, “He’s still getting injections?” Palit replied, “Yes, one for the liver every week. I’ll stop after two more. Well then—good night. You’re still here, so we’ll surely meet again—”

He had just started to leave when I saw Inspector Ratikanta Chowdhury enter through the main door. He wore the police uniform, only missing his cap. There was a trace of urgency about him. Standing by the door, he glanced around the room, then, spotting Dr. Palit, quickly came over to us.

“Dr. Palit, I have some bad news. There’s been a theft at your dispensary.” “A theft!” Ratikanta said, “Yes. Around nine o’clock, I was leaving the station to come here when I noticed the dispensary door was open. Going closer, I saw the lock was broken. Inside, your desk drawer was open—the thief broke it and made off with the cash. I’ve left a constable there. You should go. Was there any money in the drawer?” Palit, bewildered, said, “Money! There’s never much at night, at most two or four rupees.” “Still, you should go. If anything besides money is missing, you’ll be able to tell.” “I’ll go at once.” “And if anything else is missing, send a report to the station tonight.”

Shakuntala and Pandeyji, who had been conversing at a distance, noticed our agitation and came over. Pandeyji asked, “What’s happened?” Dr. Palit did not stop; he hurried away. Ratikanta explained about the theft. Then, turning to Shakuntala, he said, “I’m terribly late—will I still get dinner?” Shakuntala smiled slightly. “Of course. Come with me.”
The master of the house had already retired for the night. We took our leave of Shakuntala and left the house.
Bohni - Patanga 519 We returned.
Three
The next morning, at around nine o’clock, a motorcar arrived and stopped in front of our house. Byomkesh, lifting his face from the newspaper, furrowed his brow. “Pandeyji—so early!”
A moment later, Pandeyji entered our baithak-khana. Dressed in police uniform, his face grave. In response to Byomkesh’s questioning gaze, he said, “Dipnarayan Singh has died.”
We stared at him, dumbfounded, as if the words had not quite sunk in.
“Died?”
“Ratikanta just telephoned. This morning, Dr. Palit had come to give Dipnarayan Singh an injection. The moment the injection was administered, he died. I am going there now. Will you come?”
Without a word, Byomkesh threw his shawl over his shoulder. I too rose.
“Let’s go.”

As the motorcar rattled along, the scenes of last night replayed in my mind. I had seen Dipnarayan Singh only once, but had taken a liking to him; a courteous, smiling gentleman, who seemed to be recovering from his illness. What had happened, so suddenly? And Shakuntala—
Shakuntala was now a widow... Somehow, I could not bring myself to accept this cruel truth.

We reached our destination. Three or so cars stood parked by the gate. Pandeyji halted the car and got down. Passing through the gateway, we arrived at the main entrance of the house. The garden was deserted; a tense hush seemed to hang over everything.
At the main door, Inspector Ratikanta saluted Pandeyji with a grave face. Seeing us, his eyebrows rose slightly, but without a word, he led us all inside.

Before the door of the hall, the divan-like seat stood as before, and upon it lay the body of Dipnarayan Singh. Seated beside the corpse, Dr. Palit stared fixedly at the dead man’s face. There was no one else in the room; only the furniture remained arranged as it had been the previous night.

We tiptoed to the side of the divan. Dipnarayan Singh looked just as he had last night; death’s touch had wrought no change in his form. Eyes closed, the muscles of his face relaxed; as if he had simply fallen asleep.

Dr. Palit was so absorbed in gazing at the dead man’s face that he did not seem to notice our arrival. It was only at Pandeyji’s gentle touch that he started from his reverie. Rising, he looked at each of us in turn, then said, “A post-mortem is necessary. And—keep this vial.” Near his hand was a small brown bottle with a rubber stopper; he handed it to Pandeyji. Pandeyji held the vial up to the light—there was still about half of the liquid left inside. He handed the vial to Ratikanta and said quietly to the doctor, “Come, let’s go sit over there.”
Dr. Palit picked up his handbag from the divan. We all went and sat on a nearby sofa set. Ratikanta remained standing. Pandeyji asked—
Byomkesh Samagra
He asked, “Where is everyone else in the house?”
Ratikanta replied, “I’ve sent them all upstairs. Miss Manna is with Shakuntala Devi.”
“Miss Manna? The lady doctor?”
Palit said, “Yes. She’s the regular doctor for this house as well. Seeing Shakuntala’s condition, I telephoned her and had her brought over.”
“You did the right thing. Any news of Debnarayan?”

“Debnarayan is an idiot—he’s bawling like a child. Dewan Gangadhar Banshi is with him. Poor Chandni is the one in real trouble, she’s weeping herself, running to her husband one moment, then rushing to Shakuntala the next.” He sighed deeply.
Pandeyji remained silent for a while, then said, “Doctor Palit, please tell us everything from the beginning.”

The doctor set his bag down from his lap and said, “There isn’t much to tell. Around eight o’clock, I arrived and found Dipnarayan Babu sitting on that couch, waiting for me. Seeing me, he smiled and said—‘Didn’t expect you to come so early in this cold, have some tea.’ I said—‘Alright, but let me give you the injection first.’ Chandni was present, Shakuntala wasn’t there today. I checked Dipnarayan Babu’s pulse—it was quite good. Then I filled the syringe with liver extract and gave him the injection in his arm. It was an intramuscular injection, nothing complicated. But Dipnarayan Babu slowly slumped over. I saw his eyelids growing heavy, closing; he tried to speak but couldn’t. Immediately, I gave him adrenaline, then began artificial respiration. But it was no use—within three or four minutes, his lungs ceased to function.”

The doctor ran his fingers over his chest and fell silent. He was an experienced physician; sudden death was nothing new to him. Yet the shock he had suffered within broke through his stern composure.
Pandeyji asked, “You couldn’t determine the cause of death?”
The doctor replied, “From the symptoms, I thought—anaphylactic shock. But now I see that’s not it.”
“Then what could it be?”
“I can’t say for sure. Perhaps some kind of poison.”
Pandeyji turned his gaze to Byomkesh. Byomkesh said, “Could it have been curare poison?”
The doctor stared at him, eyes wide, then, half to himself, muttered, “Curare! It’s possible. But until there’s a post-mortem, nothing can be said for certain.”
“If he died from curare poisoning, will the post-mortem reveal it?”
“It will. It can be detected in the kidneys.”
Byomkesh asked, “Doctor, the vial you just handed to Pandeyji—what is it?”

The doctor replied, “That’s the liver extract vial. It contains ten doses of the medicine, the mouth of the vial is sealed with rubber. The syringe needle is inserted through the rubber to draw out as much medicine as needed. Today, I took the dose from that very vial and gave the injection.”
Byomkesh said, “Since death occurred immediately after the injection, it can be assumed that—”
Bahni - Page 521
“It’s possible that the injection itself was the cause of death. So, was there poison in that vial?”
The doctor replied, “What else could it be? Yet—just yesterday evening, I gave an injection to a patient from that very vial, and he’s perfectly fine.”
“Does the vial always stay in your bag?”
“Yes. When one runs out, I replace it with a new vial.”
“All right, tell me, where was your bag last night?”
“It was in the dispensary.”
“When you get a call at night, what do you do? Do you take the bag from the dispensary to visit the patient?”
“No, I keep another bag at home. If there’s a call at night, I take that one.”
“I see. So, when the thief broke into your dispensary last night, this bag was there?”

“Yes.” The doctor started, surprised—“Last night, around seven o’clock, I returned to the dispensary after seeing a patient. There was no time to go home, so I left the bag, told the compounder to lock up, and came straight here.”
“Oh—” Byomkesh pondered for a moment. “Do you know when the compounder locked up the dispensary and left?”
“Of course I do. After hearing about the theft last night, I came back here and sent for the compounder. He said he locked up the clinic and went home right after seven.”
“Very well, have you found out if anything else was stolen from the dispensary?”
“Nothing else was taken. Just a few rupees and some small change from the desk drawer.”
Byomkesh turned his gaze from Pandeyji to Ratikanta and said in a calm voice, “Then the real purpose of the theft is clear.”

Ratikanta had been listening to Byomkesh’s questions and answers with furrowed brow. Perhaps he did not like that an outsider was asking the very questions the police ought to ask. But since Byomkesh was Pandeyji’s friend, he had remained silent. Now, in a rather dry tone, he said, “What purpose is clear?”
Byomkesh replied, “Don’t you see? The thief didn’t come to steal money. He came to switch the liver extract vial.”
Pandeyji said, “Switched it?”

“Or perhaps injected a few drops of liquid curare into the doctor’s vial with a syringe. The result is the same. The thief knew that this morning, Dipnarayan Singh would be given an injection. —Now do you understand?”
For a moment, we all fell silent. Then Pandeyji asked, “Who knew that the injection would be given this morning?”
The doctor said, “Everyone in the house knew. On Sunday mornings, the injection is always given. I give it to him first, then go out to see my patients.”
Byomkesh said, “I knew as well, last night. The doctor had mentioned it. So, no one can be ruled out on that count.”
Inspector Ratikanta spoke up, leaning over the back of Pandeyji’s chair from behind, “Sir—”
BYOMKESH SAMAGRA
At first, I thought it might have been an accidental death, that Dr. Palit had mistakenly injected the wrong medicine. But now it seems— I want to take charge of this case.”

Pandeyji said, “Of course, it’s your jurisdiction! You take charge. Send the body for post-mortem immediately. And send that vial of medicine to the laboratory for analysis. This matter must be resolved.”

Byomkesh lay sprawled on the taktaposh, reading a book of poetry. I was thinking to myself, Look at him, the poet—dusk is upon us. These days, with the coming of spring, my heart grows strangely wistful. Age is catching up.

Satyabati said, “No, no, outside Calcutta. Somewhere like—Kashmir—or—”
